title: Stack vs heap: where your variables live

visuals.title: Match each memory area to its job

pairs.meaning: Local variables and parameters. Automatic, very fast, small. Freed when the function returns
Big area for memory you request while the program runs. You must give it back yourself
Global and static variables. Created once, live until the program ends
The machine instructions of your program
The stack runs out of room, for example with endless recursion or a huge local array
Heap memory you took but never gave back

visuals.title: The life of a function call on the stack

stages.name: 1. Call
stages.detail: A function is called. A new frame is pushed on top of the stack.

stages.name: 2. Make locals
stages.detail: The frame holds the parameters and the local variables. They are created automatically.

stages.name: 3. Run
stages.detail: The function body runs. Any function it calls gets a new frame on top.

stages.name: 4. Return
stages.detail: The frame is popped off the stack. All its variables are destroyed automatically.

stages.name: 5. Back to caller
stages.detail: The caller continues. The last frame in is always the first one out.

goal: After this you can name the memory areas of a running program, say where globals, locals and dynamic data live, explain stack frames, compare the stack and the heap, and describe stack overflow and memory leak in simple words.
warmup: In the canteen the plates are in a pile. You can only take the top plate and put a used plate back on top: nobody organises it, it just works, and it is very fast. That is the stack. The heap is like a big warehouse at the back: you go to the manager, ask for space, and you must return it when you finish. If you forget, the space stays blocked for nobody.
definition: When your program runs, the computer gives it memory divided into areas. The STACK holds local variables and function parameters. It is automatic: a function gets its own block (a stack frame) when it is called, and the block is freed when the function returns. It is very fast but small (a few MB). The HEAP is a big area for memory that you request while the program is running, with the new operator. It is manual: you must give it back yourself with delete. Global and static variables live in a third area that exists for the whole run of the program, and the code itself is in a fourth.
howItWorks: Step through the first trace. addOne() is called three times. Its local variable is created on the stack each time and destroyed at the end of each call, so it prints 1 every time. The static variable kept and the global total are NOT on the stack: they live for the whole program, so they keep counting 1, 2, 3. Now the second trace shows several function calls stacked up: main calls first, first calls second, second calls third. The call stack panel shows the frames piling up and then leaving in reverse order: the last frame in is the first out. Because each function has its own frame, each has its own variables (a, b, c) that cannot be seen by the others. In the third example (and the memory visual) a value is needed AFTER the function that made it has finished. A plain local is copied out by return, which is fine for small values. For big data or data that must live longer, the program can ask the heap for a box with new int. The pointer p is a local variable on the stack and disappears, but the box on the heap stays until you delete it. Do not worry about new and delete yet: the next lesson teaches them properly. Two classic problems: a STACK OVERFLOW happens when the stack becomes full, for example a function that calls itself forever (infinite recursion) or a huge local array; the program crashes. A MEMORY LEAK happens when you take heap memory and never give it back; the program slowly eats more and more memory. We never run those two in the lesson, because they are bugs.

worked.problem: Show where three kinds of variables live. addOne() has a local variable, a static variable and uses a global one. Call it three times and print all three each time. Explain why they behave differently.
pseudocode: START
global total = 0 (exists all the time)
CALL addOne() three times; each call: local = 0 (new box), kept (made once), then local++, kept++, total++
PRINT local, kept and total
END
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B["Global total = 0"]
  B --> C["Call addOne()"]
  C --> D["local = 0 (new on stack)"]
  D --> E["local++, kept++, total++"]
  E --> F[/Print local, kept, total/]
  F --> G{More calls?}
  G -- Yes --> C
  G -- No --> H([End])

sample.title: Local, static and global variables across calls
sample.expectedOutput:
local = 1, kept = 1, total = 1
local = 1, kept = 2, total = 2
local = 1, kept = 3, total = 3

explanation.text: A global variable: created before main, lives until the program ends.
A normal local variable: a fresh box on the stack at every call, destroyed at every return.
A static local: created once in the static area and keeps its value between calls (Week 7).
Only the current copy of local changes.
local is always 1; kept and total grow.
Three separate calls. After each one the stack frame of addOne disappears.

steps.note: The global total was created before main started and lives until the program ends.
Call 1: a new stack frame appears. local is a NEW box (0). kept is made ONCE in the static area, with the starting value 0.
local, kept and total all became 1.
Call 2: the old frame was removed when call 1 returned, so local was destroyed. A fresh local starts again at 0. kept still remembers 1.
local is 1 again (fresh box), but kept grew to 2 and total to 2.
Call 3: yet another new local, 0 again.
local = 1 once more, while kept = 3 and total = 3 keep counting across calls.
All calls are finished. Only main's frame is left on the stack.

worked.problem: Show the stack of function calls: main calls first(), first calls second(), second calls third(). Each prints a line before and after the inner call. Predict the order of the lines and watch the frames in the trace.
pseudocode: START main
CALL first(): push frame, a = 1, print
CALL second(): push frame, b = 2, print
CALL third(): push frame, c = 3, print, RETURN (pop)
second prints its end line, RETURN (pop)
first prints its end line, RETURN (pop)
END
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start main]) --> B[Call first]
  B --> C[Call second]
  C --> D[Call third]
  D --> E[/Print third line/]
  E --> F[Return to second]
  F --> G[/Print second end line/]
  G --> H[Return to first]
  H --> I[/Print first end line/]
  I --> J([End])

sample.title: Frames pile up and leave in reverse order
sample.expectedOutput:
first: before
second: before
third: c = 3
second: after, b = 2
first: after, a = 1

explanation.text: third() is the innermost function; its frame is the top of the stack while it runs.
c lives in third's frame only. No other function can see it.
second() has its own b.
The call to third(): a new frame is pushed. second waits.
second continues here after third returned. Its b is still 2.
first() has its own a.
The call to second(): another frame.
main starts the chain by calling first().

steps.note: main starts. The stack has one frame: main().
first() is called: a new frame is pushed on top. It holds its own a.
first prints its first line.
first calls second(): another frame is pushed on top.
second prints its first line.
second calls third(): the third frame is pushed. Now 4 frames are on the stack.
third prints. It is the top frame, so it runs.
third finishes: its frame is popped and c is destroyed automatically. Control goes back to second, just after the call.
second still remembers its own b = 2.
second finishes: its frame is popped.
first prints, still remembering a = 1.
first finishes: popped. The last frame in was the first to leave (last in, first out).
main returns and the program ends.

worked.problem: Exam style: a value must be used in main after the function that created it has ended. Show (a) a plain local returned by value and (b) a box taken from the heap with new and returned as a pointer, then change the heap value through another function. Note: new and delete are explained fully in the next lesson.
pseudocode: START
makeCopy: local x = 42 on the stack, RETURN its value (a copy); x is destroyed
makeOnHeap: ask the heap for an int box, store 42 in it, RETURN its address
main: a gets the copy, b gets the address
PRINT a and the heap value
addTen(b): add 10 to the heap box
PRINT the heap value, then delete the box
END
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B["a = makeCopy() (stack copy)"]
  B --> C["b = makeOnHeap() (heap box)"]
  C --> D[/Print a and *b/]
  D --> E["addTen(b)"]
  E --> F[/Print *b/]
  F --> G["delete b"]
  G --> H([End])

sample.title: A stack copy and a heap box that outlive their functions
sample.expectedOutput:
Copy from the stack: 42
Value on the heap: 42
After addTen: 52

explanation.text: x is a stack variable. Its value is copied out by return; the box x itself dies at the closing brace.
new int asks the heap for one int box and gives back its address. (Next lesson.)
*p = 42 stores a number in the heap box.
We return the ADDRESS. The pointer p dies with the frame, but the heap box lives on.
addTen works on the caller's heap box through the address it receives.
a holds a copy of the number.
b holds the address of the heap box.
The heap value is still there, after makeOnHeap has finished.
delete gives the heap box back. Forgetting it would be a memory leak.

variations.when: Allocated automatically on a call, freed automatically on return. Very fast. Small and fixed size (a few MB). Size known at compile time.
You allocate and free it yourself. Large, limited by RAM. Slower. Size can be decided while the program runs. Needs delete.
variations.example: int *p = new int;   delete p;   // next lesson

variations.when: Created before main, live until the program ends, visible to all functions. Use sparingly.
Created once, keep their value between calls, visible only inside the function.
Stack overflow: endless recursion or a huge local array uses up the stack and the program crashes.
Memory leak (forgot delete) or a dangling pointer (using memory after it was freed).

mistakes.error: g++ warns: address of local variable 'x' returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]. x lives on the stack and is destroyed when the function returns, so the returned address points to a dead box (a dangling pointer). Return the value, or use the heap.
No compiler error. The box on the heap is never given back: a memory leak. The pointer p dies at the end of f, so the address is lost forever.
This compiles, but when run every call adds a new frame to the stack and none is removed, until the stack is full: a stack overflow and the program crashes. (We do not run it here.)

examTips: Learn the table: stack = automatic, small, fast, freed on return; heap = manual (new/delete), large, slower, you must free it.
Name three kinds of variables and where they live: local on the stack, new boxes on the heap, global and static for the whole run.
In a stack trace question the last function called is on top, and it is the first one to finish (last in, first out).
Define stack overflow (stack full, e.g. infinite recursion) and memory leak (heap memory never given back) in one simple sentence each.
Never return the address of a local variable: the local is destroyed when the function ends.
romanSummary: Stack mein local variables aur function parameters hote hain. Yeh automatic hai, tez hai, chhota hai, aur function khatam hone par khud free ho jata hai.
Heap bara area hai jahan new se memory mangte hain. Yeh manual hai, delete se khud wapas karna parta hai.
Global aur static variables poore program tak zinda rehte hain, local variable har call par naya banta aur khatam hota hai.
Stack overflow tab hota hai jab stack bhar jaye, jaise function khud ko bar bar bulaye (infinite recursion).
Memory leak tab hota hai jab heap se memory li lekin delete nahi kiya, to woh memory wapas nahi aati.

practice.prompt: Where do ordinary local variables of a function live?
practice.hint: Think of the pile of plates.
practice.explanation: Local variables and parameters are created in the function's stack frame and destroyed when the function returns.

practice.prompt: Who is responsible for freeing memory taken from the heap?
options: The operating system after every line
practice.hint: The heap is like the warehouse where you return things yourself.
practice.explanation: Stack memory is freed automatically. Heap memory stays until you give it back with delete (or delete[]).

practice.hint: Which of a and b is created again at every call?
practice.explanation: a is a new stack box each call, so it is 1 both times. b is static: it keeps its value, so it is 1 then 2.

practice.hint: There are two different variables called count.
practice.explanation: up() has its own local count that hides the global one. The global count is never changed, so main prints 10.

practice.prompt: Which of these can cause a stack overflow?
options: Forgetting to delete a heap box
A function that keeps calling itself with no stopping case
practice.answer: A function that keeps calling itself with no stopping case
practice.explanation: Every call pushes a new frame on the stack. Endless recursion never pops them, so the stack fills up and the program crashes.

practice.hint: Return the value, not the address.
practice.explanation: Returning the value copies 5 to the caller. The box x is destroyed, but the copy lives on, so this is safe.

practice.prompt:
Fill in the blank with 'stack' or 'heap'.

Memory taken with new is on the ____ and must be freed with delete.
practice.hint: Which area is the big warehouse?
practice.explanation: new takes memory from the heap. The stack is freed automatically.

options: A variable that is too large
Heap memory that was taken but never given back
Using a variable before setting it
A function that returns too early
practice.answer: Heap memory that was taken but never given back
practice.explanation: If you take memory with new and never use delete, it stays reserved until the program ends, and the program uses more and more memory.

quiz.prompt: Which area is automatic, very fast and small?
quiz.explanation: The stack is managed automatically by function calls and is small and fast.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a function's local variables when it returns?
options: They stay for the whole program
quiz.explanation: The frame is popped from the stack, so all locals disappear.

quiz.prompt: main calls f, and f calls g. Which function's frame is on top of the stack while g runs?
quiz.hint: The most recent call is on top.
quiz.explanation: Last in, first out: g was called last, so its frame is on top and it finishes first.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the heap is true?
options: It is freed automatically when a function returns
It is smaller than the stack
It is large but you must free the memory yourself
quiz.answer: It is large but you must free the memory yourself
quiz.explanation: The heap is big, slower than the stack, and manual: you use delete.

options: for the whole program but is visible only inside its function
quiz.answer: for the whole program but is visible only inside its function
quiz.explanation: A static local is created once and keeps its value between calls, but its name can be used only in its own function.
